summary:
Hotspot Calendar turns 26 years of NASA FIRMS active-fire detections for the whole world (658 million detections) into one consistent record and shows it as a burning activity calendar for any area on Earth that a user draws on a map.

The record is split between two sensor generations: MODIS (since 2000, 1 km pixels, near the end of its life) and VIIRS (since 2012, 375 m pixels). VIIRS sees about six times as many fires, so the raw counts jump at 2012 and cannot be compared. We harmonize both onto the VIIRS scale: for the years both sensors flew, we measured how many hotspots VIIRS saw per MODIS hotspot, and we use these ratios, calibrated separately for 205 regions of the world, to translate the MODIS-only years. Tested on years the model had never seen, the world's monthly total is off by 4 % on average and a single region's month by about 12 %, and every translated value is shown with the range in which the true value most likely lies.

The web app shows which months and years burned most since November 2000, compares the current month with its historical median, maps the hotspots, and offers CSV downloads. It updates every hour from near-real-time data. Suomi NPP stopped on 2 November 2026 and MODIS will follow; NOAA-20 continues the series on the same scale.

Why it matters: fire managers ask "is this month unusual here?". That question needs a record whose numbers mean the same thing in 2003 and in 2026, whichever satellite was in orbit.
details:
REPO: https://git.reazer.net/nasa-space-apps/harmonization-of-modis-and-viirs-hot-spots

WHAT IT DOES

Hotspot Calendar is a web app for early warning and emergency responders, scientists and land managers. A user draws an area anywhere on Earth (rectangle, circle or polygon), or simply moves the map, and gets:

  • a fire calendar, year by month from November 2000 to yesterday, coloured by hotspot count, with months far above or below what is usual for that time of year marked;
  • a year comparison that ranks the years by fire activity;
  • the current month compared with the historical median of the same days in earlier years;
  • a map of harmonized hotspot density or of the single detections of all five satellites;
  • downloads: the hotspots of a search as CSV, calendar values as CSV, calendar and map as images.

All counts are on one scale, so the sensor of origin no longer matters.

HOW IT WORKS

  1. One reference scale. We chose VIIRS on Suomi NPP (375 m). From February 2012 its detections are counted as measured.
  2. Translating MODIS. For 2012-2019, when MODIS and VIIRS flew together, we calibrated the ratio of VIIRS to MODIS hotspots per calendar month and for day and night, separately for each of 205 regions of the world. In our California deep dive they range from about 2 (winter days) to 16 (September nights): at night VIIRS sees many small fires that MODIS misses. For the years before 2012 these ratios turn MODIS counts, per 0.25 degree cell and month, into VIIRS equivalents. The result is distributed as a weight onto the individual MODIS detections, so any area, any day and any filter is answered by the same weighted sum, and calendar, map and comparison always agree.
  3. Closing the gaps. Suomi NPP repeatedly delivered no data (for example on 11 days in July 2024, during the Park Fire) and stopped on 2 November 2026. Missing overpasses and everything since then are counted from NOAA-20, which carries the same instrument, scaled per region with factors calibrated on overpasses both satellites observed. Without this, 58 % of California's July 2024 detections would be missing; worldwide, NOAA-20 supplies 6-8 % of the detections in 2022, 2024 and 2026.
  4. Honest uncertainty. Estimated years are marked in the app. Each estimated value carries a 90 % range, calibrated per area size and per filter by cross-validation.

VALIDATION

Calibrated on 2012-2019 and tested on unseen years (2020 to July 2026). Worldwide, on 16,195 region-months: the mean absolute error was 12.3 % of the observed total per region and month, and 4.1 % for the world's monthly total (95 % of the months within 10 %), with a bias of -1.7 %. The 90 % range contained 85 % of the region-months (95 % weighted by detections). Small, quiet regions are less exact: the median region misses by 23 %, and the regions above 30 % hold 3 % of all detections.

Our California deep dive (a single-region build with MODIS 2000-2017 from the FIRMS API, 79 test months): the mean absolute error was 1,006 detections, equivalent to 12.6 % of the average observed monthly count (7,961). Almost all of the error comes from the translation itself, not from missing input data: in the 70 test months with complete MODIS data the error is 12.0 %. As an independent check, the models for the two MODIS satellites, applied separately to 2003-2011, agree within 9 % per year.

LIMITS

Quality differs between regions; small regions with few fires to calibrate on are coarse, and a few tiles with almost no fires (Antarctica, open ocean; 0.0001 % of all detections) belong to no model region. Large areas are slow on our small server (a calendar for the whole world takes 7-15 seconds), so the app asks before loading them. The live data still use an older FIRMS classification of industrial sources for MODIS 2000-2017 (only our California deep dive uses the newer one). Before 2012 all values are estimates; the model from Terra, used only for November 2000 to August 2002, is weaker (20.9 % error, bias -11.3 %). The 90 % range is calibrated per region; for areas that span many regions, such as a continent or the whole world, it is still far too wide. Industrial heat sources before 2012 cannot be estimated from MODIS and are assumed constant. The method has not yet been reviewed by an independent expert.

BENEFITS

  • An emergency manager sees within seconds whether the current month is unusual for an area, against 26 years instead of the 15 years that VIIRS alone provides.
  • Trends and rankings of fire years are no longer distorted by the change of sensor in 2012.
  • The record does not end with MODIS or Suomi NPP: it continues with NOAA-20 and NOAA-21.
  • Everything is open: data from NASA FIRMS, code under Apache 2.0, a documented API (OpenAPI 3.1).

WHAT WE HOPE TO ACHIEVE

A fire calendar that any agency can use for its own region, anywhere on Earth. The next steps are one processing version of the MODIS data for the whole world, faster views of whole continents, a model that borrows from neighbouring regions where fires are rare, and a review of the method by fire scientists. Within the app: official fire reports next to the detected hotspots (for the US from FPA FOD and NIFC), counts of fire events instead of hotspots, and an outlook of the critical months ahead based on the harmonized history.

TOOLS AND LANGUAGES

Backend: Python 3.12, DuckDB, pandas, statsmodels, SciPy, Shapely, FastAPI; data stored as Parquet. Frontend: TypeScript, Vue 3, Vite, MapLibre GL JS, Terra Draw, TanStack Query. Operations: Docker, nginx, Caddy, GitLab CI/CD; an hourly job fetches FIRMS near-real-time data. Source code, tests (100 backend, 74 frontend) and the full list of open-source components with licenses: https://git.reazer.net/nasa-space-apps/harmonization-of-modis-and-viirs-hot-spots

TEAM

It works on my ChatGPT: Sebastian Appel (backend: data pipeline, harmonization, validation, API, server) and Sandro Sauer (frontend: web app, map, calendar, design). Everything else is shared.

WHY THIS CHALLENGE

We chose this challenge because we wanted to build something that goes beyond solving an interesting technical problem.

As software developers, we are naturally drawn to complex challenges. Working with decades of satellite data, understanding the differences between sensors, and finding a way to make their measurements comparable was exactly the kind of problem we wanted to tackle.

But for us, the purpose behind the technology mattered just as much.

One of our team members has family roots in Portugal, a country that has repeatedly suffered from devastating wildfires. Seeing the impact these fires can have on communities, nature, and people's lives makes this challenge feel much more personal.

It made us ask ourselves a simple question: How can we use our skills to create something that might actually help people?

We believe that making historical fire activity easier to understand is one step in that direction. By bringing more than two decades of satellite observations onto a comparable scale, we hope to help researchers, communities, and decision-makers better understand long-term patterns and unusual fire activity.

We know that our application cannot prevent wildfires or predict exactly where the next one will occur. But we believe that accessible, transparent, and reliable information can contribute to better research, awareness, and informed decisions.

For us, this project is about more than code, algorithms, or satellite data. It's about using technology to turn complex information into knowledge that could make a difference.
